title: Did survival actually improve?
hook: Move the diagnosis date while keeping the death date fixed.

knows: arithmetic means, rates and simple plotted values
doesNotKnow: earlier diagnosis lengthens "survival time" even if death comes on the same day.

misconception: Treating lead-time bias as valid without checking the stated model, denominators or causal assumptions.
objective: earlier diagnosis lengthens "survival time" even if death comes on the same day.
keyState: Both finite cases completed; their computed summaries retained.

claims.text: In both toy worlds death is at year 10. Diagnosis is at year 8 without screening and year 5 with screening. How much does recorded post-diagnosis survival increase?
claims.source: src/demos/probability/p100-lead-time-bias/spec.ts; exact finite illustration specified in manager numericCase: Symptom diagnosis at year8, screened diagnosis at year5, death year10 in both worlds. claims.text: Moving the starting line changes elapsed time after diagnosis without changing lifespan. A survival-time comparison can therefore improve even when mortality is unchanged. These dates illustrate the arithmetic, not an actual screening program.

claims.text: Diagnosis moves from year 6 to year 4, death stays year 9. What happens to lifespan? Post-diagnosis survival increases from 3 to 5, but the stipulated death date and lifespan do not change.

provenance.difference: New teaching boundary: Lead-time bias. Existing boundary: The learner can explain that in a group of 14 whose deaths do not move, finding the illness 3 years earlier raises 'alive 5 years after diagnosis' from 6 to 12 because only the start of the clock moved (lead time), and that comparing deaths in whole groups is not fooled by this.
